rect.title: This diagram is drawn from ply.yaml, the file describing this codebase's architecture and verification claims. Each box is a component; chips are functions with their declared checks; arrows are permitted calls (solid) and data flows (dashed); red bars are forbidden calls. A box's grey depth is how strongly it promises to be checked — white means something inside promises nothing, deeper grey means stronger checks promised, and the weakest function sets the whole box's shade. Nothing here is green: green is kept for evidence a run has actually earned, which this render never sees, so a picture full of promises should not look like a picture full of results. Hover anything for its meaning.

g.title: ply.yaml — the document this picture is drawn from. Everything you see here was declared in it; nothing was inferred from code. What each box has actually been checked for is what `cargo ply verify` reports, not this drawing. ply: 1 — the format version every rule below is read under; a version this build does not speak is refused, never guessed at

What this document declares. "0 functions promise nothing" counts functions that end up with nothing checked -- whether nobody wrote any checks for them, or the document switched checking off for them on purpose. Running `cargo ply verify` is what turns promises into results; this line never reports results.

component cli — maps to Rust module ply_cli The library behind `cargo-ply`. Its shell -- argument parsing, file I/O, subprocess calls -- is deliberately unclaimed; what is claimed is the logic those commands share. state Cli — the structure this component holds. The rows below are its fields: each name was found in the code, and each shape read off what that field really is declares checks up to fuzzed — checked against many random inputs — the strongest verdict this could earn if every declared check ran and passed; a promise, never a result this box is this shade because `join_plainly` is the weakest thing in it: it declares fuzzed — checked against many random inputs — nothing here is drawn stronger than its weakest part

command — one of the things this component holds; the two overlapping outlines mean a structure of your own -- there is more inside it than this row shows. Written in the code as `Commands`. The name came from the document; the shape and the type came from the code, so this row cannot say something the source does not. The hatching means Ply has no way to make one of these, which is usually why the functions around it come back unchecked.

json — one of the things this component holds; the filled block means one single value -- a number, a flag, a character. Written in the code as `bool`. The name came from the document; the shape and the type came from the code, so this row cannot say something the source does not.

The one command that produces evidence rather than describing intent. state VerificationResult — the structure this component holds. is_local fuzz(256) — tries 256 generated inputs that satisfy requires, then checks ensures input and post contract: Postcondition (ensures): |result| *result == local_module_path(&local_anchors, &anchor).is_some() the checks above are what will test the function against exactly this promise when `cargo ply verify` runs

local_module_path fuzz(256) — tries 256 generated inputs that satisfy requires, then checks ensures test — runs the declared examples plus generated cases; each case must satisfy the function's requires and ensures input and post contract: Postcondition (ensures): |result| !local_anchors.is_empty() || *result == Some(String::new()) the checks above are what will test the function against exactly this promise when `cargo ply verify` runs 3 worked examples — the `test` check above compiles each into a test when `cargo ply verify` runs; a promise of what will run, never a result
